title: Faith in Mind, whole
tomorrow: flowers fall even when we love them. so then what?

lines: TWENTY MINUTES TO PICK A SHOW.
THE GREAT WAY IS NOT DIFFICULT.
cards: Two good options, and the deciding takes longer than either would. Twenty minutes of scrolling to pick a show, then no time to watch it. An old Chan poem names this as the whole trouble.

Faith in Mind, the Xinxin Ming, opens, in paraphrase: the great way is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose. Read whole, in one sitting, the poem keeps returning to that line. But what does it ask?
Readers in Chan and Zen have heard it two ways.

teach.b: The first reading takes the line all the way. The poem says that when love and hate are both gone, everything becomes clear.
It says a hair's breadth of difference sets heaven and earth apart, and that setting what you like against what you dislike is the mind's sickness.
So the practice is to drop preference itself, to meet whatever comes without ranking it. Its best case: the poem means it. Half measures leave the war running in the background.
The second reading says the poem isn't against choosing; it's against the grip. Readers here point to the poem's own advice: don't seek the true, just stop holding on to opinions.

Choices still get made; a cook still picks the ripe fruit. What drops is the clinging, the replaying, the war after the decision. Its best case: it's livable, and it fits the poem's warning against chasing even emptiness.
And where the two meet is the poem's ending. When the mind doesn't divide, the poem says, there is not two.
Both readings land there: not two, not me against the moment.

teach.h: THE WAY ISN'T THE HARD PART.
teach.b: One reading gets there by dropping preference; the other by holding it lightly enough that it stops being a fight. Either way, the poem's promise is the same. The great way is not difficult.
The difficulty is in the picking and choosing, and the endless back and forth.

how: Some Chan and Zen communities chant the Xinxin Ming or study it line by line; teachers differ in how strictly they read its call to drop preference.

o: a guide to building trust between a teacher and student
a Chan poem on the way, where picking and choosing is the snag
a Chinese creed listing what every believer must accept

games.q: two readings, one poem — tap the pairs.

s: the Xinxin Ming says the great way is very difficult
it says the great way is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose.

some hear it as dropping preference itself; others as choosing without clinging.

games.q: your friend says the poem means: have no preferences at all, ever. what's the strongest case for her reading?
o: the poem means it: half measures leave the war running inside.
she just doesn't want to make decisions, so she found a verse.
the poem is too old to say anything about real choices now.
games.why: that's her side at its best: the poem names like-against-dislike as the mind's sickness. the other side agrees about the war and keeps the choice.

practice: Settle into a position and decide not to adjust it for the whole sit. An itch, a stiff knee, a sound you'd rather not hear: notice the pull to fix it, and let it be as it is.
No choosing better and worse for two minutes, just this, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Faith in Mind, the Xinxin Ming: a Chan poem credited by tradition to Sengcan, read today as a whole. Its first line: the great way isn't difficult for those who don't pick and choose.

orig.note: Chinese (xinxin ming): faith or trust (信), mind (心), inscription (銘): the poem's title.

carryVoice: Keep this one: no picking and choosing, or at least, no war after you choose. A whole poem, in one sitting.
